title: The Grand Inquisitor
where: *The Brothers Karamazov*, Part II, Book V, Chapter 5
about: Ivan Karamazov, twenty-three, sits in a tavern with his brother Alyosha, twenty and a novice in a monastery. Alyosha has just said that there is a Being who can forgive everything, and Ivan tells him a story he made up about a year ago and calls a poem. In Seville in the sixteenth century Christ comes back for a moment, and the Grand Inquisitor, a cardinal of almost ninety, has him arrested and comes alone at night to the prison. The English is Constance Garnett’s, of 1912.

view.says: Auden wrote that the evidence for Satan’s argument, when he holds out the world’s kingdoms to Jesus, is perhaps nowhere put so fully and forcefully as by the Grand Inquisitor. Jesus gives him no answer, as he gave none to Satan or to Pilate, because none is needed. Such men are answered by their own experience. They know they have failed, and that knowledge, with the hatred they have stirred up, makes them cry out.
view.quote: their own experience answers for them and they know very well what they do, and that they have failed
view.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), p. 51
view.checked: Both sentences are quoted in remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 18 (c) and the appendix (lines 1056 and 1174: PD pp. 50–51; also as quoted by Mendelson, Early Auden, Later Auden, p. 395, citing PD 51 and Prose II 435). The cry and its two causes (the knowledge of failure, and the hatred such men meet) and the place of the sentence in Auden’s account of the third temptation are from the summary in remake/research/E_pd_pearce.md, sections 1.2 and 1.3, which also fixes the page: p. 50 ends in the middle of the sentence about loving no one, and the Grand Inquisitor is first named about the middle of p. 51. Both notes read again on 2026-10-03. Earlier in this session the two sentences were also read in full-text-search snippets of the Internet Archive scan of the Ecco Press edition, with the foot line of p. 51 after them; those snippets could not be read a second time. Examiner, 2026-10-03: read again, twice, in the same scan (Internet Archive item prolificdevourer00aude, full-text-search snippets chained one to the next). Page numbers stand at the foot in this book (the foot line of p. 26 comes just before the heading of Part II, which the contents put at p. 27). Seen: the foot line of p. 50 in the middle of the sentence before these two, about loving no one; both sentences word for word, and the quotation is exact; the second sentence running on through the knowledge of failure and the hate aroused to the cry, which Auden quotes loosely as far as the refusal of love (hosted block 20, words 1047 to 1075); then the sentence on the attendant, after which the foot line of p. 51 follows. Mendelson, Early Auden, Later Auden (2017), p. 395, read in the full text at the Internet Archive, quotes the same passage through the first question of the cry. Finisher, 2026-10-03: p. 51 was read from its first words to its last in search snippets of the same scan, chained one to the next (remake/works/karamazov/finisher/pdread.py prints them and keeps nothing). The sentence before the one on the evidence is Auden’s comment that Satan, by claiming the kingdoms are his to give to Jesus, claims to be God; so the view now names that offer where it had “the third temptation”, a term the page had not yet explained, and the whole view stands on p. 51. Tested with build/tools/runs.py against p. 51 stitched in memory: the old wording shared a run of five words with him (the two words before the old man’s title, and the title); the new wording shares no run over four.

plates.heading: The first words in the prison

lenses.label: Questions
lenses.name: hypophora
lenses.plain: a speaker asks a question and at once answers it himself
lenses.caption: The old man asks four questions here. The first, asked twice, gets no reply, and he forbids one: Don’t answer, be silent. After each of the others he goes straight on with a statement of his own. To ask and answer oneself is an old figure of argument, hypophora; one form of it asks an opponent what he can say: What canst Thou say, indeed? Of a later question Ivan tells Alyosha that the old man asks it and answers the question for Him. The old man’s reason for the silence is that the Prisoner has no right to add anything. Auden’s is that Jesus does not need to answer.
lenses.why: Dostoevsky has the old man forbid an answer and supply his own, and has Ivan say so; the old man holds that the Prisoner has no right to add anything, and Auden that he has no need to answer.

grounds.claim: Four questions, the first asked twice; after each of the other three he goes on with a statement of his own

grounds.claim: Asking and at once answering one’s own question is a figure of reasoning, and an old one; in one form the speaker asks an adversary what can be said
grounds.source: Gideon O. Burton, Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), entry anthypophora: a figure of reasoning in which one asks and then immediately answers one’s own questions; it sometimes takes the form of asking the audience or one’s adversary what can be said on a matter. The entry lists hypophora, subjectio and rogatio among its other names and cites the Ad Herennium 4.23.33-4.24.34 (subjectio), Peacham 1577 (hypophora) and Puttenham 1589. The entry hypophora reads: see anthypophora. Both opened and read again 2026-10-03.

lenses.label: Voices
lenses.what: Who speaks in the chapter, and inside whose speech

facts.counted: Counted on the hosted text karamazov/b05c05 with the site’s word-splitter (site/js/kit/syllables.js, tokens) by a script that gives each word to a voice by the quotation marks around it. Outside all marks: the narrator. Inside double marks: Ivan or Alyosha, whoever the paragraph belongs to. Inside single marks within Ivan’s paragraphs: the Grand Inquisitor in blocks 8, 12, 14, 17 to 21 and 31 (but not the 39 words of the Jesuits that Ivan quotes in block 12, words 45 to 53 and 56 to 85); the Prisoner for words 303 and 304 of block 6; otherwise the other voices Ivan quotes. Sayings of Christ that Ivan or the old man quotes from Scripture are counted as quotations, with the one who quotes them, and not as words of the Prisoner. The 261 words the old man himself quotes are part of his 4,988; the 9 words Alyosha quotes are part of his 507. The two verse quotations Ivan recites (blocks 1 and 3, 38 words) are counted with the other voices he quotes. Two words joined by a dash count once (there are 42 such words in the chapter), and a row of points that stands alone is joined by the splitter to the word before it and is not counted; there are seven such rows (blocks 24, twice, and 26, 31, 36, 37 and 42), so the total is 9,244 where the index of the hosted text, which counts by spaces, says 9,251. Checked: the six voices add up to 9,244, and the 56 rows of “paragraphs” add up to the same six totals.
facts.key: In “voices”, “inside” names the voice in whose speech this one is heard, by its short name. In “paragraphs”, n is the paragraph’s place in the chapter (its block number plus one; n 2 and n 4 are the two verse quotations), and each other entry is the number of words a voice speaks in that paragraph, under the voice’s short name. Paragraph 9 (block 8) holds the passage shown, paragraph 21 (block 20) the cry, paragraph 32 (block 31) the kiss. Alyosha’s four interruptions are paragraphs 10, 12, 14 and 16; the unbroken run is paragraphs 17 to 22.

lenses.caption: Of the chapter’s 9,244 words Ivan speaks 8,343, and inside his telling the old man speaks 4,988, more than half the chapter. Auden wrote that the evidence for Satan’s argument is perhaps nowhere put so fully and forcefully as by the Grand Inquisitor. Ivan says beforehand that in his poem Christ says nothing. He gives the Prisoner two words, said to a dead child before the arrest, and in the prison none; in the Russian the two are Aramaic, as Mark’s gospel gives them. Alyosha breaks in four times; after that nobody interrupts for 4,527 words. At the first interruption Ivan tells him that the one thing that counts is for the old man to have his say.
lenses.why: Ivan gives the old man more than half the chapter and the Prisoner two words, and says the one thing that counts is for the old man to have his say; Auden finds Satan’s case perhaps nowhere more fully put.

lenses.label: Word

notes.source: The Russian text (Nauka, 1991, at ilibrary.ru); Wiktionary, Russian entry ты: (familiar) second-person singular, you, thou; a count of Thou, Thee, Thy, Thine, Thyself and one lower-case thee on the hosted text, each read in its place

notes.note: From an Old English word for harming or checking, built on a root that means behind. Five times the speech speaks of the Prisoner’s coming to hinder them, the last time as the reason for burning him.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, hinder (v.): Old English hindrian, to harm, injure, impair, check, repress; a derivative verb from a root meaning on that side of, behind; thus the ground sense is to put or keep back. The five places: block 8, words 50 and 57; block 14, word 154; block 20, word 1053; block 21, word 930. The Russian verb is the same in all five (Wiktionary, мешать: to hinder, to impede, to prevent, to interfere with).

notes.note: He says he does not know, and does not care to know, whether this is Christ or only a likeness of him. Two thirds of the way through the speech he asks whether he does not know to whom he is speaking.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, semblance: from Old French semblance, likeness, appearance; the meaning person or thing that resembles another is attested from the 1510s. Wiktionary, Russian entry подобие: similarity; semblance, likeness. The later question: block 20, words 1093 to 1100, which is word 3,328 of a speech of 4,977.

notes.note: The Russian word is the same Greek one.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, heretic: from Greek hairetikos, able to choose, verbal adjective of hairein, to take; heresy: Greek hairesis, a taking or choosing for oneself, a choice. Wiktionary, Russian entry еретик: borrowed from Old Church Slavonic, from Ancient Greek hairetikos. The complaint: block 19, words 456 to 490 and 641 to 669.

lenses.caption: The old man says Thou twelve times here and Thee twice. The Russian has its ordinary familiar pronoun, which the brothers also use. Garnett gives the brothers you and keeps thou, long since a word of church and literary English, for what is said to Christ and God: 220 times in the chapter, and for no one else. So in her English the threat of burning comes in the pronoun of the chapter’s prayers. The threat names the Prisoner among the heretics, a word from the Greek for one able to choose. Later in the speech the old man complains that the Prisoner left men the fearful burden of free choice.
lenses.why: Garnett keeps thou for Christ and God alone, so in English the old man threatens the Prisoner in the pronoun of the chapter’s prayers; and the word for those he burns means, at root, one who chooses.

pair.label: From the opening of the speech

lenses.label: Sentences
lenses.caption: These hundred words are eleven sentences: five questions, two commands and four statements, the last of them the secret. In the rest of the old man’s long argument a sentence averages 23 words; here, nine. The first two questions ask why, and no answer follows either. The first command is Be angry. The later questions he answers himself, and one answer is that whatever he has to tell is known to Thee already. Then he tells the secret, which nobody has asked for. The short questions are Dostoevsky’s; the two commands are sentences of their own only in Garnett’s English. Auden quotes the opening of these lines as the cry of men who know they have failed.
lenses.why: A long argument breaks into short questions and commands put to a silent listener, and the secret comes out unasked; Auden quotes the opening of these lines as the cry of men who know they have failed.

grounds.claim: Eleven sentences in a hundred words: five questions, two commands, four statements, of 8, 14, 2, 10, 12, 8, 10, 11, 11, 2 and 12 words

lenses.label: Earlier

ties.say: The same question, almost word for word. The first time he went straight on with a statement of his own. This time another question follows.
He ordered this silence himself. Now he asks why the Prisoner looks at him silently.
Early on he remarks that the Prisoner looks at him meekly and will not even be angry. Now he asks why, and orders him to be angry. In the Russian *meekly* and *mild* are forms of one word.
At first it was the old man who knew too well what the Prisoner would say. Now it is the Prisoner who knows all that he can say.

lenses.caption: The other lines shown come from the opening of the speech, about three thousand words earlier. There the old man forbids an answer, says he knows too well what the Prisoner would say, and remarks that the Prisoner looks at him meekly and will not even be angry. Here each of these comes back turned around, and in between the Prisoner has not spoken. Auden holds that such men are answered by their own experience.
lenses.why: The old man’s opening terms come back turned around after about three thousand words in which the Prisoner has said nothing; Auden holds that such men are answered by their own experience.

The Russian text (Nauka, 1991, at ilibrary.ru) has тайна at all eleven places where block 20 has mystery, and Garnett has secret for the same word in block 19 (words 38, 242 and 402) and block 21 (words 450 and 492). lenses.caption: The paragraph has used mystery six times before these lines. It is one of the three powers the old man names, miracle, mystery and authority, and it is what the people must follow blindly. Here it is the rulers’ own. Our mystery is what they hide: that they work with the tempter and not with Christ. The Russian word means both a mystery and a secret, and Garnett keeps mystery throughout the paragraph. After the poem Alyosha gives his own account of it: the old man has no belief in God, that’s his secret, and Ivan agrees.
lenses.why: The word that named one of the Church’s three powers over the people here names what the rulers hide, that they work with the tempter; afterward Alyosha calls the secret unbelief, and Ivan agrees.

lenses.caption: The old man’s speech runs 4,977 words from its first question to its last word, the Latin Dixi, with which an orator closed a speech. He builds the speech on the three temptations in the wilderness, in Matthew’s order: bread, the pinnacle of the temple, the kingdoms of the earth. These hundred words stand between the second and the third, and their secret leads into the third: his Church, he goes on, took from the tempter the last gift the Prisoner refused. Auden names the Grand Inquisitor in his account of that temptation. The words hinder us come five times in the speech, the last time as the reason for the burning.
lenses.why: The speech follows the three temptations in order, and the secret told in these lines opens the third, the gift the Prisoner refused and the Church took; it is at the third that Auden names the Grand Inquisitor.

lenses.label: Answer
lenses.caption: The old man wants words: he longed for Him to say something. Auden writes that Jesus gives him no answer, having no need to. What comes is a kiss, told in one sentence of eighteen words, and then five words that name it: That was all His answer. The Prisoner’s verbs are approached, kissed and went away, none of them a verb of speech. The old man, after 4,977 words, says eleven more and lets out the man he was to burn. The sentences are as short in the Russian. Asked what becomes of the old man, Ivan says: The kiss glows in his heart, and his idea stays as it was.
lenses.why: The old man wants words and gets one act, which the story calls all the answer; after 4,977 words he says eleven more, lets the Prisoner go, and keeps his idea. Auden holds that Jesus has no need to answer.

ties.say: Each kiss comes where words were asked for. The old man longs for the Prisoner to say something. Ivan asks Alyosha a question.
Each kiss comes out of a silence. In the Russian Alyosha also kisses him *silently*, a word Garnett leaves out.
The same act in nearly the same words. The Russian has an old poetic word for the old man’s lips and the everyday word for Ivan’s.
The old man says *go* and never come again. Ivan asks for the kiss once more and then says *go*, in the Russian the same word.
Alyosha asks whether Ivan is with the old man. Ivan says that Alyosha’s kiss comes from the Prisoner’s.

lenses.caption: When the poem is over Alyosha asks Ivan And you with him, you too? Later Ivan asks whether Alyosha will renounce him, and Alyosha does what the Prisoner did: he softly kissed him on the lips, in the Russian with the same adverb and verb. Ivan names it at once: You stole that from my poem. Alyosha’s question sets Ivan beside the old man, and Ivan’s remark on the kiss sets Alyosha beside the Prisoner. The old man shudders at the kiss and says come no more. Ivan is highly delighted, and at parting asks to be kissed once more.
lenses.why: Dostoevsky has the poem’s one listener answer Ivan with the Prisoner’s kiss, in the same words, and has Ivan say where it comes from; the old man sends the Prisoner away for good, and Ivan asks for the kiss again.

lenses.caption: Four words of the ending go back to earlier places in the chapter. The Prisoner kisses softly, as he came softly and spoke softly to the dead child. The word answer goes back to the old man’s first words, which met no answer and forbade one. Where Garnett writes aged lips Dostoevsky has ninety-year-old lips. The old man is almost ninety, and by Ivan’s account he has kept silent for ninety years. Where she writes glows Dostoevsky has burns. At the Prisoner’s coming it is love that burns in His heart; at the end, in the same Russian verb and noun, the kiss burns on the old man’s heart.
lenses.why: The ending repeats words from earlier in the chapter: those of the Prisoner’s quiet coming, the forbidden answer, the old man’s ninety years and the love burning in the Prisoner’s heart; Garnett’s English keeps two of the four.

auden.says: Auden’s account of the temptations in the wilderness stands under a sentence from this chapter, signed Dostoyevsky: the old man’s remark that the three questions gather up the whole of mankind’s later history. Auden reads them as the temptations of childhood, of adolescence and of maturity. In the third, he says, Satan appeals to reason: truth is tested by success or failure, people love only themselves, and so the true way lies in being stronger than one’s neighbor. By claiming that he can give the kingdoms, Auden adds, Satan claims to be God.
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 48–51
auden.checked: remake/research/E_pd_pearce.md, sections 1.2 and 1.3, a summary made from search snippets of the Internet Archive scan; read 2026-10-03. Pages 48 to 50 were not seen by me. Examiner, 2026-10-03, in search snippets of the same scan (prolificdevourer00aude): the epigraph, which opens with the three questions, carries a parenthesis of Auden’s naming the temptations in the wilderness and is signed Dostoyevsky (it is the sentence at hosted block 17, word 267, quoted loosely); the first temptation called that of childhood and the second that of adolescence; the third, the temptation of maturity, beginning with the last words of p. 49; Satan’s speech on p. 50 and the head of p. 51 (he appeals to reason; the test is the experience of success or failure; the true way is to be stronger than one’s neighbor, since people love only themselves); and Auden’s comment after it on p. 51, that Satan in claiming to be able to offer the kingdoms is claiming to be God. The poet’s wording, that Satan argues from experience that every man loves only himself, was brought nearer to this. Finisher, 2026-10-03: the entry was held against the places it reports, read again in snippets of the same scan (remake/works/karamazov/finisher/pdruns.py: the counting of build/tools/runs.py, with words broken at a line’s end closed up). It shared three runs of five words or more with Auden’s text: six with his parenthesis in the epigraph (words 5 to 10 of the entry as it stood), five in Satan’s speech (words 73 to 77) and six in the comment after it on p. 51 (the entry’s last six words). Each was said again with nothing added: the number dropped from the first, the verb changed in the second and the tense in the third. Tested again after the change: see the finisher’s section of notes.md.

auden.says: Auden then writes the answer Jesus might have made if he had been listening to an attendant who only repeated his master’s words, and not to the Inquisitor. It takes up three of the old man’s sentences in turn: that men find nothing harder to bear than freedom, that the wish to worship in common is their chief misery, and that the Church has corrected Christ’s work and rested it on miracle, mystery and authority. The freedom Jesus holds out, the answer says, is freedom to know what is true, and each person must find that by his own faith and effort.
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 51–58
auden.checked: remake/research/E_pd_pearce.md, sections 1.3 and 1.4 (summary, with the three headings quoted), read 2026-10-03. The sentence on the attendant, on p. 51, was among the snippets read earlier in this session; pp. 52 to 58 were not seen by me. Examiner, 2026-10-03, in search snippets of the Internet Archive scan: the sentence on the attendant, the last on p. 51; the three sentences of the old man that head the parts of the reply, each quoted loosely (they answer to hosted block 18 from word 56, block 19 from word 142 and block 20 from word 974); the freedom offered, called the same that the Inquisitor professes to offer and the only one there is, the freedom to know the truth; no other way to the truth but individual faith and individual effort; and the last words of the reply with the foot line of p. 58 after them, just before the heading of Part III. Finisher, 2026-10-03: the last sentence of p. 51 and the passages on freedom and on faith and effort were read again in snippets of the scan and the entry held against them (finisher/pdruns.py). The critic’s new order of the first sentence had made a run of five words with Auden’s (the entry’s words 26 to 30 as it stood; the scan breaks the last of them at a line’s end, which hides the run from build/tools/runs.py). The last word of the five was dropped; nothing else in the entry shares a run over four with what was read.

auden.says: In that answer Jesus says that the Inquisitor, and not he, has turned the Last Supper into a mystery. Later in the book Auden states what history must show if Jesus was right: a general movement toward unity and equality, which the way of love has always helped, and which the way of hatred and force has always hindered and has always failed in the end to prevent. If history does not show it, he writes, then Jesus was mistaken and the right lay with Satan and the Inquisitor.
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 54 and 62
auden.checked: remake/research/E_pd_pearce.md, sections 1.2 and 1.4, read 2026-10-03. Not seen by me. Examiner, 2026-10-03, in search snippets of the Internet Archive scan: the remark on the Last Supper closes the second part of the reply, after the foot line of p. 53 and before that of p. 54; on p. 62, after the foot line of p. 61, come the Way of love and understanding, which must always have assisted events so to move, the Way of hate and coercion, which must have always hindered them and always failed finally to prevent them, and then the sentence on Satan and the Inquisitor, which begins from history not offering this evidence. The direction itself is set out just before, at the foot of p. 61: the unity of mankind, and equality with it. The poet’s wording, that his account of the two Ways is not borne out by history, was made exact from these. Finisher, 2026-10-03: p. 62 from the foot line of p. 61 to the end of the sentence on Satan and the Inquisitor, and the remark on p. 54, were read again in snippets of the scan and the entry held against them (finisher/pdruns.py). Making the wording exact had left a run of six of Auden’s words, his name for the second Way (words 51 to 56 of the entry as it stood). Its two nouns were said again in plainer words, hatred and force; no run over four is left.

auden.says: Charles Miller, a student in the class who also shared Auden’s house, gives Auden’s words at the first meeting, in early October 1941, as he reconstructs them. Auden named *The Brothers Karamazov* among the great books the students would be examined on, with the *Divine Comedy*, Augustine’s *Confessions* and four plays of Shakespeare. No record has been found of what he said in class about the novel.
auden.source: Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), pp. 26–27
auden.checked: remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, the appendix (line 1140: Miller pp. 26–27, from an OCR snippet), and line 1009 for the absence of any record of a class on Dostoevsky; remake/research/A_michigan_course.md, lines 25, 204 and 265, for Miller, the reconstruction and the date. Read 2026-10-03. Miller’s book was not opened by me. Examiner, 2026-10-03, in search snippets of the Internet Archive scan (audenamericanfri00mill): the date and the classroom, and the speech with the four titles in the order given here (the scan garbles the novel’s name, so a search for it finds nothing). The page was not seen as an image; the book’s own index gives Dostoyevsky at pp. 19, 26 and 89, Augustine at p. 26 and Dante at pp. 26–27, which puts the naming of the novel on p. 26 and the account of the meeting on pp. 26–27.

auden.says: In the spring of 1943 Auden put a chart on the table of his seminar on Romanticism at Swarthmore College. In its row for the hero it lists the Grand Inquisitor with Iago and Stavrogin under The Demonic Villain, in the column headed “Hell of the Pure Word,” knowledge without power.
auden.source: Chart of 1943, reproduced in Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (2017), pp. 554–55
auden.checked: remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 18 (line 475) and the appendix (lines 1019 and 1071): read by the researcher from a scan of the reproduction, who says the placing of the name in that column is his own reading; remake/research/B_pedagogy.md, 1.W2, for the seminar. Read 2026-10-03. Not seen by me. Examiner, 2026-10-03: Mendelson’s full text at the Internet Archive read at p. 554 (in the spring of 1943 Auden was teaching a seminar at Swarthmore that the printed catalogue called Romanticism, and one day, without comment, he put the diagram on the seminar table; the note to p. 554 says the chart is transcribed from the more polished of two copies, now in Swarthmore College Library), and the image of p. 555 fetched and looked at. The chart has a column of row names at the left and three columns: Hell of the Pure Deed, This World, Hell of the Pure Word (Knowledge without Power). In the row Hero the last column reads The Demonic Villain, a line about sex appeal, then Iago, Stavrogin, The Grand Inquisitor, and a last line about master-crooks. So the placing is plain on the page, and the hedge that it was the researcher’s reading was taken out of the entry. Finisher, 2026-10-03: the chart’s cells read in the full text of Mendelson’s book at the Internet Archive (item early-auden-later-auden-a-critical-biography-edward-mendelson-2017, the lines that follow the page mark 554). The last column is headed Hell, of, the Pure Word on three lines, with Knowledge without Power on the line under them, as the first is headed Hell of the Pure Deed with Power without Purpose under it; the cell reads The Demonic Villain, a line on sex appeal, Iago, Stavrogin, The Grand Inquisitor and a line on master-crooks. The two labels are Auden’s own words, three and five of them. The heading of the column was a run of five of his words outside a quotation, and the critic found that a reader could not tell where it ended; it now stands in quotation marks, the second quotation of the piece after the one in the view. The three-word label keeps its capitals, as the examiner set it (quotation marks were tried on it too and taken off again, so that the piece holds two quotations and no more). No word was changed.

caveats: Auden’s view is from *The Prolific and the Devourer*, written in 1939 and not published by him, which was read here only in search snippets of a scanned copy. No mention of the kiss was found in it, so the third passage cites him only for the Prisoner’s silence.
Nothing Auden said about the novel in the 1941 class is on record. That he named it at the first meeting comes from a student’s memoir written about forty years later.

The English is Constance Garnett’s. She sometimes cuts Dostoevsky’s sentences shorter, tells the kiss in the past tense where he uses the present, and does not always keep his repeated words (*aged* for ninety-year-old, *glows* for burns).

The counts follow the text printed here. A row of dots is not counted as a word, two words joined by a dash count as one, the quotation marks decide who speaks each word, and a sentence ends at a period, question mark or exclamation mark before a capital.
The figure in the first passage has several names. The handbook used here lists it under anthypophora and gives hypophora, the name Peacham used for it in 1577, as another.
open: Nothing by Auden on the kiss, on Alyosha’s kiss, or on any part of the novel outside this chapter was found in the research notes (the third and fourth leads in pieces.json). The third passage therefore keeps to the text and the Russian; only its tab Answer cites him, and only for the Prisoner’s silence (see the examiner’s entry below).

The Russian was read in an online copy of the 1991 Nauka edition (ilibrary.ru) and at Russian Wikisource, not in the first edition of 1880. The capital letters Garnett gives to pronouns for Christ were not compared with any Russian edition, and the piece says nothing about them. No Russian text is hosted, so no Russian is shown; every Russian fact is given as a gloss or a note.

That heretic comes from the Greek for one able to choose is a fact of the word; nothing read says Dostoevsky meant the link with free choice, and the caption gives the two facts in two sentences, the second with its place in the speech, and draws no conclusion from them (loosened by the finisher, 2026-10-03).

The sentence counts rest on Garnett’s punctuation and on one rule for the end of a sentence (given in the caveats). The parts of the speech in the Plan follow the paragraphs of the text printed here; in the Russian copy read the long argument is one paragraph.

On the second and third passages a second set of lines is given as the “pair” for one tab only (Earlier, Again): two cuts from two paragraphs of the opening, and five short paragraphs from the brothers’ later talk. The plates do not set “beside”, so that, as the kit now works for another passage of the same work, those lines show only on the tab that marks them. The two sets have different numbers of rows (1 and 2, 4 and 5), so they are never set line under line; if the rows are ever changed so that the numbers are equal, “beside”: true must be set. The page has since been built and photographed by the examiner and the critic; the examiner found the second set of lines only on its own tab, beside the passage at 1280 px and under it at 390 px, with numbered underlines and no strokes across.

From the examiner (the poet’s three entries that this one overtook were taken out by the finisher): I read The Prolific and the Devourer myself in full-text-search snippets of the Internet Archive scan (prolificdevourer00aude), which answer as often as they are asked, about fifteen words at a time: pp. 48 to 51 nearly whole, the three sentences that head the parts of the reply, its passages on freedom, the remark on the Last Supper (p. 54), its last words (p. 58), and the two conditions and the sentence on p. 62. Everything the piece gives as Auden’s was found there at the page given. A full copy has still not been seen, and what lies between the snippets was not read. Mendelson was read in the full text at the Internet Archive (pp. 351 note, 395, 554 and its note, the list of abbreviations) and the image of p. 555 was looked at; New Year Letter and Miller were read in snippets of their scans.

From the examiner: the year of the Ecco Press book is not settled, and the question touches every piece that cites it. The catalog record of the first trade edition (Open Library OL1395108M, built from the Library of Congress record, LCCN 93002409) and the Internet Archive’s record of the scanned copy give 1994. The cataloging data printed in the book carries 1993 in its call number, the book prints no other year for this edition, and Mendelson’s list of abbreviations cites the Ecco Press edition as 1993. The piece keeps 1994. The contents page says Preface by Edward Mendelson and the book nowhere says edited by, so the sources now say with a preface by.

From the examiner, for the research notes and for other pieces: the note to line 1566 in New Year Letter (Faber, 1941) is on p. 153, not pp. 152–53, because in that book the page number stands at the foot (the same note holds the sentence about how most American books might begin, which a piece on Moby-Dick may cite). Auden’s two adverbs for the Grand Inquisitor are joined by and. In Mendelson’s reproduction of the 1943 chart the Grand Inquisitor stands plainly in the row Hero, in the column Hell of the Pure Word (Knowledge without Power), under The Demonic Villain, between Stavrogin and a last line about master-crooks; the placing is not a matter of reading the scan. Miller’s page was not seen as an image: his index gives Dostoyevsky at pp. 19, 26 and 89, Augustine at p. 26 and Dante at pp. 26–27.

From the examiner: the third passage now cites Auden once, on the tab Answer and in its why, for the silence only: Jesus gives the Inquisitor no answer, having no need to. A search of the scan of his book finds no form of the word kiss, and Ivan and Alyosha are not named in it; the first caveat tells the reader so.

From the examiner: the figure’s name was tested against the first passage. Only the last of the four questions is answered in its own terms (what will be tomorrow). The second is the form the handbook describes in which a speaker asks an adversary what he can say; after the third the old man repeats his charge. So the parts are labeled as statements of his own, not as answers, and the caption rests the name on the handbook and on Ivan’s own words about a later question. Two captions set two facts side by side and claim no link that a source makes: heretics and free choice (Words), the ninety-year-old lips and the ninety years of silence (Russian). Each fact was checked; no source read says Dostoevsky meant either link.

From the finisher, 2026-10-03: three entries of the poet’s that the examiner’s reading overtook, and the examiner’s account of the morning’s builds, were taken out of this list; the page has been built again from the reading as it now stands, and every tab changed since the critic was photographed at 1280 and 390 px, with the whole page (remake/works/karamazov/shots/finisher). What changed, and why, is at the end of notes.md. In short: the view names Satan’s offer of the kingdoms where it had the third temptation; the captions of Words and Russian give their two facts in separate sentences; the entry on the note in New Year Letter was taken out of the list and is kept whole at the end of notes.md, with its line in the sources; on Mystery the last note’s mark covers word 1146 alone; five strings of the two drawn tabs were set; and seven runs of five or six of Auden’s own words (one each in the view, the caption of Voices and the second and third entries of the list, three in the first entry) were said again in the page’s words, with the five-word heading of his chart put in quotation marks. The Prolific and the Devourer is not among the scans on this machine, so build/tools/runs-sweep.py cannot hold the page against it. The places the page reports were held against search snippets of the Internet Archive scan instead (finisher/pdruns.py): p. 51 whole, and elsewhere only the places the list reports (the epigraph and the names of the first and third temptations, Satan’s speech, the remark on the Last Supper, the sentences on freedom and on faith and effort, and the two Ways with the sentence after them). The rest of the book was not tested. The caption of Plan names the three temptations in the wilderness in the same six words as Auden’s parenthesis in his epigraph on p. 48; they are the common name of the episode, the sentence does not report him, and it was left.
